methods.label: Determine when an allowed real y exists
methods.explanation:
The denominator requires \(y\ne0\). Multiplying by \(y\) gives
\[
x(y-1)=y^2.
\]
In particular, \(y=1\) is impossible, so \(x=y^2/(y-1)\). To find the possible outputs \(x\), rearrange this relation as a quadratic in \(y\):
\[
y^2-xy+x=0.
\]
A proposed value of \(x\) can work only if this quadratic has a real root. Its discriminant must therefore satisfy
\[
x^2-4x=x(x-4)\ge0.
\]
The two factors have the same sign, or one is zero, exactly when \(x\le0\) or \(x\ge4\).

We must still check the original denominator. At \(x=0\), the quadratic becomes \(y^2=0\), forcing \(y=0\), which is forbidden. At \(x=4\), it gives \((y-2)^2=0\), and \((x,y)=(4,2)\) satisfies the original equation.

For every \(x<0\) or \(x\ge4\), the discriminant is nonnegative, so a real root exists. Such a root cannot be \(0\), because the quadratic has value \(x\ne0\) there, or \(1\), because its value there is \(1\). Reversing the algebra therefore gives an original solution. The exact attainable range is
\[
x<0\quad\text{or}\quad x\ge4.
\]
Every solution consequently satisfies the necessary bound in choice A. Its included endpoint \(x=0\) is not attainable.
